query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys containing both passivating elements (such as Cr and Al) and fast diffusing, non‐protective elements (such as Mn), a high density of grain boundaries promotes a selective, accelerated outward diffusion of Cr and Al. This leads to the early formation and long‐term retention of a continuous, adherent protective oxide layer that resists further oxidation, whereas a coarse‐grained microstructure permits excessive outward transport of Mn and other volatile elements, resulting in non‐protective, porous scales.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a balanced composition of passivating elements (e.g., Cr, Al) and elements prone to forming non-protective oxides (e.g., Mn), prepared in two distinct microstructural states: one as-cast (coarse grains) and one processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained (high grain-boundary density) structure.
generation.intervention: Expose both microstructural variants to high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 1100 °C in air) for extended durations (beyond 200 hours), while employing in situ and ex situ characterization techniques (e.g., TGA, XRD, SEM/EDS, TEM) to monitor oxide scale formation and evolution.
generation.conditions: Oxidizing atmosphere at 1100 °C (1 atm oxygen) with exposure time of at least 200 hours; comparison between samples with ultrafine-grained (high grain-boundary density) versus conventional coarse-grained microstructures.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary density, which modulates the effective diffusion paths for both passivating elements (Cr, Al) and rapidly diffusing elements (Mn).
generation.mechanism: The enhanced grain-boundary diffusion in the ultrafine-grained alloy preferentially transports Cr and Al to the surface, leading to rapid nucleation and growth of a continuous, adherent Cr/Al-rich protective oxide. In contrast, the coarse-grained state allows significant diffusion of Mn and other non-protective species to the surface, resulting in porous or non-uniform oxide scales that spall easily.
generation.predicted_outcome: Ultrafine-grained (high GB density) samples will display lower mass gains, form a uniform, continuous Cr/Al-rich protective oxide scale, and exhibit enhanced resistance to spallation compared to their as-cast coarse-grained counterparts. The coercively formed scale will act as an effective barrier against oxygen ingress, substantially slowing down further oxidation.
generation.baseline: The as-cast coarse-grained high-entropy alloy, known from prior studies to form less protective, heterogeneous oxides dominated by faster-diffusing species such as Mn.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be applicable in high-entropy alloys that have sufficient content of passivating elements (Cr, Al) alongside elements with high diffusivity (Mn) and may not extend to alloys lacking such compositional contrasts or to oxidation conditions where alternative mechanisms (e.g., evaporation or scale volatilization) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extrapolates from findings in the NV1 alloy system (PMC6513993::web::015::discussion), which demonstrated improved protection via Cr-based oxides at higher temperatures, and from observations in processed AlCoCrFeNi alloys (PMC9026100::web::017::oxidation_kinetics) showing enhanced oxidation resistance due to ultrafine-graining. The exact quantitative balance between the diffusion rates and the threshold GB density necessary for protective scale retention remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical high-entropy alloy compositions in two microstructural states (coarse-grained and ultrafine-grained via controlled processing). Subject both sample sets to isothermal oxidation at 1100 °C in air for a test duration exceeding 200 hours. Employ in situ techniques (e.g., high-temperature XRD, TGA) along with ex situ imaging (SEM/EDS, TEM) to monitor oxide layer formation, continuity, composition, and adherence.
measurements: Mass gain over time via thermogravimetric analysis (TGA)
Oxide phase and scale thickness via in situ/high-temperature XRD
Oxide morphology and elemental distribution via SEM/EDS and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain, fail to develop a continuous and adherent Cr/Al-rich oxide layer, or show similar oxidation behavior to the coarse-grained samples, then the role of grain-boundary facilitated selective diffusion in forming a protective oxide layer is refuted.

Mn, Cr, and Fe preferentially diffused outward and became oxidized on the surface of specimens with time and temperature. In a diffusion controlled phenomenon, a linear regression model was fitted using Arrhenius curves. The slope of the curve yields the value of −Ea/R in the temperature range of 850–1050 °C, which was utilized to calculate the value of activation energy.
